The pages in this section compare the two packages with the established alternatives in their
language, on the same test functions and with the same measurements, and every figure and
number is computed from the installed versions when the site is rendered — nothing is typed
in. The scripts are the code cells themselves, folded on the pages; unfold any of them to see
exactly what was run.

## What is compared

| Page | ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against |
|:--|:--|
| [Interpolation](interpolation.qmd) | Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl, Dierckx.jl |
| [Derivatives](derivatives.qmd) | Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl, Dierckx.jl |
| [Integration](integration.qmd) | BSplineKit.jl, Dierckx.jl, NumericalIntegration.jl |
| [Nonuniform grids](nonuniform.qmd) | Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl, Dierckx.jl |
| [Smoothing](smoothing.qmd) | the package's own Gaussian, BSplineKit.jl, Dierckx.jl, FastChebInterp.jl |
| [Scattered data](scattered.qmd) | ScatteredInterpolation.jl, NaturalNeighbours.jl |
| [High dimensions](high-dimensions.qmd) | Interpolations.jl |

The Julia package is the reference implementation and has every feature, so these pages cover
everything; the [Python benchmarks](../python/index.qmd) compare the port with SciPy on the
capabilities it has, and since the port gives the same numbers as the Julia package, the
accuracy results here hold for it too.

## How

**Accuracy** is the largest absolute error against the exact function on a fine grid of test
points, as a function of the grid spacing, on Runge's function $1/(1 + 25x^2)$ on $[-1, 1]$ —
smooth, but with a narrow peak that is the classical difficulty for polynomial interpolation,
so that the convergence order only shows once the grid resolves the peak. Derivatives and
integrals are compared with the exact derivatives and integrals of the same function. Each
method is used at its own highest practical order: a cubic spline is a cubic spline, and a
B-spline package is given a high degree where it offers one.

**Time** is measured with [Chairmarks](https://github.com/LilithHafner/Chairmarks.jl), which
runs each expression repeatedly and reports the minimum; setup (constructing the interpolant)
and queries (evaluating it) are timed separately, because the packages differ in where they
spend their time: the convolution kernels compute nothing at construction beyond the boundary
values, and evaluate in constant time per point, whatever the grid size.

Timings depend on the machine. The ones on these pages were measured on:

- Julia 1.13.3 on Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700KF, 28 threads, 64 GiB



Relative timings between packages transfer to other machines better than absolute ones.

## What the comparisons do not show

The alternatives are mature, widely used packages, and the comparisons are on the ground the
convolution kernels were designed for: uniform or tensor-product grids, smooth data, high
accuracy. A package built for other ground — unstructured meshes, extrapolation, data with
discontinuities — is not worse for losing a comparison here. Where a competitor has no
counterpart for a capability (analytic integrals in constant time, exact scattered-data
interpolation with derivatives and integrals), the page says so rather than inventing a
comparison.

---

*Rendered with Julia 1.13.3 on a Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700KF machine (28 threads), with ConvolutionInterpolations.jl 1.0.2, Interpolations.jl 0.16.3, BSplineKit.jl 0.19.3, Dierckx.jl 0.5.4, FastChebInterp.jl 1.3.1, NumericalIntegration.jl 0.3.4, HCubature.jl 1.8.0, QuadGK.jl 2.11.3, ScatteredInterpolation.jl 0.3.6, NaturalNeighbours.jl 1.3.6, Chairmarks.jl 1.3.1.*
